disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by one or more non-bizarre or less obviously bizarre delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thought, or marked mood episodes that would suggest schizophrenia or a primary mood disorder with psychotic features. Outside of the delusional beliefs, functioning can be relatively preserved, and behavior often appears normal unless directly influenced by the delusional system. Onset is typically in mid to late adulthood and the course is often chronic, with beliefs remaining fixed despite clear contradictory evidence and limited insight. Subtypes may center on themes such as persecution, jealousy, erotomania, or somatic concerns, and clinicians distinguish delusional disorder from culturally sanctioned beliefs by assessing idiosyncrasy, rigidity, and the degree of functional impairment or interpersonal conflict produced by the delusions.

narrative.stressor: Around eighteen months ago, as Loretta’s adult children became more independent and she shifted her energy into choir, community walking groups, and her new home-organization consulting work, she began to fixate on subtle changes in her husband’s routines and interactions at church. What started as occasional suspicion during choir practice planning meetings gradually solidified over the next year into an unshakable conviction about his supposed hidden activities, despite consistent reassurance from family and friends and no corroborating evidence. Her growing preoccupation with these beliefs began to intrude on her quilting circles and seniors walking group, where she started questioning others’ motives and declining invitations tied to her husband’s social network. The situation came to clinical attention when marital counseling with their pastor stalled over her inability to reconsider her beliefs, and the pastor, concerned about how entrenched they had become despite minimal other changes in her functioning, encouraged a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I know everyone keeps telling me I’m wrong, but I’m absolutely certain about what my husband is hiding from me, and nothing they say changes my mind.”

narrative.stressor: About fourteen months ago, during a period of restructuring at his IT department and talk of outsourcing tech support, Joselito began to interpret ordinary glitches and policy changes as part of a targeted effort against him. Over the following year, as he continued mentoring junior staff and writing for a senior tech newsletter, these ideas hardened into a fixed conviction that certain coworkers were covertly monitoring his computer projects and trying to sabotage his reputation, even when audits and HR investigations found no irregularities. His late-night over-planning and coffee-fueled troubleshooting gradually centered more on documenting perceived plots than on actual technical problems, creating tension with colleagues and minor performance concerns despite his otherwise intact skills. He finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after his wife, worried by his insistence that the company was secretly building a case to fire only him and his refusal to accept reassurances from supervisors, asked their primary care doctor for a referral.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My job says everything is fine, but I know certain people at work are secretly working against me and I can’t be convinced otherwise.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly a year and a half ago, after losing her sales job at the home-improvement store and moving back in with relatives in Douglas, Kaitlyn’s life became less structured, with more time spent on social media, local political debates, and sporadic karaoke nights. During this transition she latched onto an online conspiracy thread related to local politics, and over the next fourteen months her beliefs about being personally targeted by certain community figures and neighbors evolved from casual talk into a rigid, all-encompassing explanation for why she hadn’t been able to hold a job or keep friendships steady. Friends from her softball league and church line-dancing group initially brushed off her comments, but as she began organizing impromptu “awareness” gatherings and confronting people she believed were involved, tensions with family and the community grew and her relatives became increasingly worried about her safety and reputation. The family ultimately sought psychiatric help after a heated incident at a karaoke fundraiser she had organized, where her unwavering insistence on these accusations disrupted the event and made it clear that her fixed beliefs were no longer just a quirky viewpoint but were seriously affecting her relationships and prospects.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Everyone keeps saying I’m overreacting, but I know certain people in town are targeting me, and nothing anyone shows me changes what I know is true.”
